misconceptions.label: Rounds an angle to the nearest right or straight angle
misconceptions.description: The student sees an angle that is close to $90^{\circ}$ or close to a straight line and names it a right angle or a straight angle, instead of checking whether it is exactly that size.

refutation.text_md: You noticed how close the angle is to $90^{\circ}$ (or to a straight line), and comparing with those sizes is the right habit. The slip is treating "close to" as "equal to".
A right angle is exactly $90^{\circ}$, and a straight angle is exactly $180^{\circ}$. An angle that is even one degree more or less is a different type.
An angle of $91^{\circ}$ is bigger than $90^{\circ}$ and smaller than $180^{\circ}$, so it is an obtuse angle, not a right angle.
In the same way, $210^{\circ}$ is more than $180^{\circ}$, so it is a reflex angle, not a straight angle. And two sides that bend, even slightly, do not make a straight line.
So ask two questions: is it exactly $90^{\circ}$? Is it exactly $180^{\circ}$? If not, decide whether it is less than or more than each of them, and name it from that.

The refutation is mathematically correct and matches the canonical answers (91 degrees is obtuse, 210 degrees is reflex). It argues against the error, 'close to' treated as 'equal to', and not only the method. It has no q: ids, figure references or review history. The signal's clause 'straight angle for 210 degrees' is not a near-miss: 210 is 30 degrees past straight, so that answer is more likely straight/reflex confusion than rounding. The signal would therefore sometimes misdiagnose, hence signal_ok false.

misconceptions.label: Calls every angle wider than a right angle obtuse
misconceptions.description: The student knows an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle but forgets that it must also be smaller than a straight angle, so a straight angle or a reflex angle gets called obtuse.
misconceptions.signal: Answers obtuse angle for a straight line, for an angle of $180^{\circ}$, or for an angle of $210^{\circ}$.

refutation.text_md: You are right that an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle. What is missing is the upper limit: an obtuse angle must also be smaller than a straight angle.
An obtuse angle is bigger than $90^{\circ}$ and smaller than $180^{\circ}$. An angle of exactly $180^{\circ}$ is a straight angle: its two sides make one straight line.
Once an angle is bigger than $180^{\circ}$ it is a reflex angle. So an angle of $210^{\circ}$ is a reflex angle, not an obtuse angle, even though it is also wider than a right angle.

Check the size against $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ in turn. Less than $90^{\circ}$ is acute, exactly $90^{\circ}$ is right, between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ is obtuse, exactly $180^{\circ}$ is straight, and more than $180^{\circ}$ is reflex.

The arc shows which angle to name. When it is drawn round the outside of the bend, going the long way from one line to the other, the angle it marks is the larger one.
That larger angle is bigger than a straight angle, so it is more than $180^{\circ}$. An angle of more than $180^{\circ}$ is a reflex angle.

Next time, trace the arc with your finger from one line to the other. If it goes the long way round, past a straight line, the angle is a reflex angle. If it stays on the inside, name it by comparing its size with $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.

misconceptions.label: Swaps the names acute and obtuse
misconceptions.description: The student judges correctly that one angle is narrow and another is wide, but attaches the names the wrong way round, calling a wide angle acute and a narrow angle obtuse.

refutation.text_md: You have judged the size correctly: one angle is narrow and the other is wide. It is the names that have been swapped, which is easy to do with two names you have to remember.

misconceptions.label: Compares the marked angles without matching their positions
misconceptions.description: The student sets the two angle sizes marked on the figure side by side, sees that they differ, and calls the lines not parallel, without first finding the angle that sits in the matching position.

refutation.text_md: You compared the two marked angle sizes, $95^\circ$ and $85^\circ$, saw that they are different, and decided the lines are not parallel. Comparing angle sizes is the right test. The trouble is that these two are not the pair the test asks about.

The test only works on a matching pair: corresponding angles or alternate interior angles (which must be equal), or co-interior angles (which must add to $180^\circ$). Two angles in different positions can differ whether or not the lines are parallel, so their being different tells you nothing.

Here the $95^\circ$ is below the upper line, on the left of the transversal (the line cutting across), and the $85^\circ$ is below the lower line, on the right of it. They are not in matching positions. Use angles on a straight line to reach the matching one: next to the $95^\circ$ is $180^\circ-95^\circ=85^\circ$, which sits below the upper line on the right of the transversal, in the same position as the marked $85^\circ$ at the lower line. Those are corresponding angles, and they are equal.

Before you compare, ask where each angle sits at its own crossing. If it is not in the matching position, use angles on a straight line to move to the one that is, then test. Here the corresponding angles are equal, so the lines are parallel.

misconceptions.label: Calls lines parallel because they look it
misconceptions.description: The student answers 'parallel' because the lines look parallel in the picture, or because the angles come out close, even though the angle test does not hold exactly.
misconceptions.signal: Writes that the angles are 'about' or 'nearly' equal, or 'close to' $180^\circ$, and answers parallel.

refutation.text_md: You went by how the lines look, or by the angles coming out close, and called them parallel. That is a natural first reaction, and it was right to look at the angles. The catch is that a drawing can look parallel when it is not.

The test is exact: two lines are parallel only if corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, or co-interior angles add up to exactly $180^\circ$. An angle that misses by a few degrees fails the test, and a few degrees is too small to see in a picture.

For example, co-interior angles of $115^\circ$ and $55^\circ$ add to $115^\circ+55^\circ=170^\circ$. That is not $180^\circ$, so those lines are not parallel, however close they look. In the same way, corresponding angles of $56^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ are not equal, so those lines are not parallel either.

Choose one pair (corresponding, alternate interior or co-interior), find both sizes (using angles on a straight line where you need to), and run the exact test. Answer 'parallel' only when the test holds exactly.

misconceptions.label: Uses only one of the two equal angles in the angle sum
misconceptions.description: In an isosceles triangle the student knows two angles are equal but writes the angle sum with only one of them, so the unknown angle comes out too big.
misconceptions.signal: Each equal angle comes out as 144 degrees when the angle between the two equal sides is 36 degrees, or 45 degrees when the three angles are $x$, $x$ and $3x$.

refutation.text_md: You spotted that two angles of the isosceles triangle are equal, which is the right start. The slip is in the sum of the angles: a triangle has three angles, so an equal angle has to be written twice, once for each corner it belongs to.

Take an isosceles triangle where the angle between the two equal sides is $36^{\circ}$ and the other two angles are both $x$. Writing $36^{\circ} + x = 180^{\circ}$ gives $x = 144^{\circ}$, and that angle appears at two corners. Check: $36^{\circ} + 144^{\circ} + 144^{\circ} = 324^{\circ}$, far more than the $180^{\circ}$ the angles of a triangle add up to.

With both equal angles in the sum, $180^{\circ} = 36^{\circ} + 2x$, so $2x = 144^{\circ}$. The $144^{\circ}$ is the two equal angles together, so it has to be shared between them: $x = 72^{\circ}$, and $36^{\circ} + 72^{\circ} + 72^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}$ checks.

Write one angle per corner in the sum, and let the equal angles appear as many times as there are equal corners. For angles $x$, $x$ and $3x$ that is $x + x + 3x = 180^{\circ}$, so $5x = 180^{\circ}$ and $x = 36^{\circ}$.

The book's answer is 72, and the 36 degree figure with x, x, 3x gives x = 36, which the refutation reproduces. Writing 36 + x = 180 gives 144, and 36 + 144 + 144 = 324 is a valid contradiction. Writing 180 = 36 + 2x gives 2x = 144 and x = 72, which is correct and fixes the book's sign typo. Writing x + 3x = 180 gives 45, which matches the signal. The refutation is mathematically right and self-contained, uses the book's angle-sum method, and names no unseen figure or question id. One caveat is that an answer of 144 could also come from forgetting to halve 2x = 144. Step 3 covers that case too, since it says the 144 is shared between the two angles, so I do not count it as misdiagnosis.

misconceptions.label: Adds the squares even when a shorter side is the unknown
misconceptions.description: The student writes $x^2 = a^2 + b^2$ with the two given lengths every time, without checking whether the unknown side is the one opposite the right angle.
misconceptions.signal: An unknown shorter side that comes out longer than the given side opposite the right angle, for example about 13.93 instead of 12 when the given sides are 13 cm and 5 cm.

refutation.text_md: You added the two squares, which is exactly right when $x$ is the side opposite the right angle. The theorem of Pythagoras has a fixed shape, though: the square of the side opposite the right angle stands alone on one side, and the squares of the other two sides are added on the other.

Try it on a right-angled triangle where the side opposite the right angle is 13 cm and another side is 5 cm. Adding gives $x^2 = 13^2 + 5^2 = 194$. Now check that against the theorem: the squares of the two sides next to the right angle should add up to $13^2 = 169$, but $194 + 5^2 = 219$. The answer fails its own check.
Put the side opposite the right angle on its own: $13^2 = x^2 + 5^2$. Then $x^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 144$, so $x = 12$ cm, and now $144 + 25 = 169$ checks.

Before you add or subtract, find the right-angle mark and ask which side is opposite it. If $x$ is that side, add the squares of the other two, as with 15 and 20 giving $x^2 = 625$ and $x = 25$. If $x$ is one of the other two sides, subtract the square of the known short side from the square of the side opposite the right angle.

misconceptions.label: Treating the angles at a meeting point as vertically opposite when the lines are not straight
misconceptions.description: The student sees two triangles touching at a point, assumes the angles there are equal because they are vertically opposite, and uses that angle as the included angle for SAS, even though the lines through the point are not straight lines.

refutation.text_md: You have two pairs of equal sides meeting at a point, and you went looking for the angle between them. That is the right instinct for SAS. The catch is the claim that the angles at that point are equal: vertically opposite angles are only equal when two **straight** lines cross.

If the sides on either side of the point do not carry on in a straight line through it, they are just sides that happen to meet there. The angles between them are not vertically opposite, and nothing given says they are equal, so you cannot use them.
Without that angle, what you really know is two equal sides in each triangle and nothing more. The book says we need at least three facts about the triangles, and two equal sides is only two facts.

Before you write "vertically opposite angles", check that both lines really are straight through the point. If you cannot show that, use only the facts you are given. If they do not complete one of SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS, the answer is "not enough information".

misconceptions.label: Writing the letters of a congruence statement in the wrong order
misconceptions.description: The student finds the right pair of triangles and the right rule, but writes the letters of one triangle in an order that does not line up with the matching corners of the other.

refutation.text_md: You have found the right pair of triangles and probably the right rule. The slip is in how the letters are written. In a congruence statement the letters are not just names: their order says which corner matches which, first with first, second with second, third with third.

Take one triangle with $90^\circ$ at $D$, $35^\circ$ at $C$ and $55^\circ$ at $E$, and another with $90^\circ$ at $B$, $35^\circ$ at $C$ and $55^\circ$ at $A$. The equal corners are $D$ with $B$, $C$ with $C$ and $E$ with $A$. Written in that order the statement is $\triangle CDE\equiv\triangle CBA$.
Change the order and the statement says something false. $\triangle CDE\equiv\triangle ABC$ would pair $C$, which is $35^\circ$, with $A$, which is $55^\circ$, and those angles are not equal.

The order also does work afterwards. From $\triangle CDE\equiv\triangle CBA$ you can read straight off that $CE=CA$, because $C$ and $E$ sit in the same places as $C$ and $A$. To write your own statement, pair up the equal angles and sides first, then write each triangle's letters in that same pairing order, and check that the first letters match, then the second, then the third.

misconceptions.label: Thinks AAA needs all three pairs of angles shown equal
misconceptions.description: The student will not accept a pair of triangles as similar by AAA unless all three pairs of angles are marked equal, so a pair with only two matching markers is rejected or left undecided.

refutation.text_md: The name AAA does suggest three angles, and you are right that similar triangles need all three pairs of corresponding angles equal. What you do not need is to be shown the third pair: two matching markers already settle it.
The angles in a triangle always add up to $180^{\circ}$. So the third angle in each triangle is what is left when the other two angles are taken away from $180^{\circ}$.

If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of the other, the same amount is taken away from $180^{\circ}$ in both triangles, so what is left must be the same in both. The third pair of angles is equal even though it carries no marker: the third angle in each triangle must be equal.

So when two corners of one triangle carry the same markers as the matching two corners of the other, treat all three pairs of angles as equal and call the triangles similar by AAA. Check that the two markers really match one for one.

misconceptions.label: Calls a pair similar without matching the angle markers
misconceptions.description: The student picks the pair of triangles that looks alike, or whose corners simply carry marks, without checking that each marker on one triangle is repeated on the corresponding corner of the other.

refutation.text_md: You chose the pair that looks like the same shape, or whose corners carry marks. Marked angles are exactly the right place to look, and a first impression is a fair start. What is still missing is the comparison: a drawing can look alike and still have different angles, so how it looks cannot decide the question.

The AAA rule asks for corresponding angles that are equal. In a diagram, equal angles carry the same marker: the same number of arcs, or the same letter. Two arcs and three arcs are different markers, so they stand for different angles, however alike the triangles look.

Take a pair where one triangle has a corner with two arcs and a corner with one arc, and the other triangle has a corner with three arcs and a corner with four arcs. Both triangles have marks at the matching corners, but no marker on one is repeated on the other. The angles are all different, so no pair of corresponding angles is equal and the triangles are not similar. The same goes for letters: corners called $a$, $b$, $c$ in one triangle and $d$, $e$, $f$ in the other share no marker, so none of the angles is shown equal.

So set the look of the triangles aside and go corner by corner. A pair of triangles is similar when the corresponding angles carry the same markers, and the pair where the same markers appear on both triangles is the one to choose.

misconceptions.label: Accepts sides that grow by different amounts as in proportion
misconceptions.description: The student sees that every side of the bigger triangle is a larger multiple of the matching side of the smaller one and calls the triangles similar, without checking that it is the same multiple for all three pairs of sides.

refutation.text_md: You noticed that every side of the bigger triangle is a longer version of the matching side of the smaller one, and that is the right thing to look at first. The check still to do is whether each side grew by the same amount.
The SSS rule needs the three pairs of corresponding sides to be in proportion. Comparing each bigger side with its matching smaller side has to give the same result all three times.

Take a small triangle with sides $x$, $y$, $z$ and a larger one with sides $2.3x$, $2.5y$, $2.2z$. Every side has grown to more than twice its length, but the three sides are $2.3$ times, $2.5$ times and $2.2$ times as long. Those are three different amounts, so the sides are not in proportion and the triangles are not similar.

Compare a larger triangle with sides $1.2x$, $1.2y$, $1.2z$. Each side is $1.2$ times the matching side, the same amount every time, so the three pairs of sides are in proportion and the triangles are similar.
So work out the comparison for each of the three pairs of matching sides, and call the triangles similar only when all three agree.

misconceptions.label: Doubts that a kite's diagonals cross at right angles
misconceptions.description: The student says the diagonals of a kite do not intersect at right angles, treating the right angle as something a lopsided shape like a kite cannot have.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'False' to a statement that the diagonals of a kite intersect at right angles.

refutation.text_md: You answered False, as if the diagonals of a kite could not cross at a right angle. A kite looks lopsided, so a right angle there is easy to doubt, but it is a property of every kite and it can be proved.

Take a kite $ABCD$ with $AD=AB$ and $CD=CB$, and let the diagonals meet at $O$. Diagonal $AC$ lies between the equal sides, so it bisects $\hat{A}$: $B\hat{A}O=D\hat{A}O$. Triangles $ADO$ and $ABO$ then have $AD=AB$, the side $AO$ in common, and these equal angles at $A$, so they are congruent (SAS). That gives $A\hat{B}O=A\hat{D}O$.

Call each of the equal angles at $A$ by the letter $t$, and call $A\hat{B}O=A\hat{D}O$ by the letter $p$. The angles of triangle $ADB$ add up to $180^\circ$, so $2t+2p=180^\circ$, which gives $t+p=90^\circ$.

Now $A\hat{O}D$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABO$, so it equals the two opposite interior angles added together: $A\hat{O}D=A\hat{B}O+B\hat{A}O=p+t=90^\circ$. So $AC\perp BD$: the diagonals of a kite do intersect at $90^\circ$, and the statement is True.

Whenever you doubt this property, check it the same way: mark the equal sides, bisect the angle between them, prove the two small triangles congruent, and use the angle sum to show the angle at the crossing point is $t+p=90^\circ$.

misconceptions.label: Mixes up what makes a rectangle, a rhombus and a square
misconceptions.description: The student has the family right (four sides, both pairs of opposite sides parallel) but lets right angles and equal sides stand in for each other or hangs them on the wrong name, so a right-angled shape with unequal sides becomes a square or a rhombus, an equal-sided shape with no right angles becomes a square or a rectangle, or the adjacent sides of a rhombus are allowed to differ.
misconceptions.signal: Square for a shape whose sides are not all equal or whose angles are not all $90^\circ$; rhombus for a shape with right angles and unequal sides; rectangle for a shape with four equal sides and no right angles; or 'true' for 'two adjacent sides of a rhombus have different lengths'.

refutation.text_md: You have the family right: four sides, with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. The mix-up is in the two checks that sort that family: 'are all the interior angles $90^\circ$?' and 'are all the sides equal in length?'. They are two separate questions, so one cannot stand in for the other, and each name uses them in its own way.

A rectangle has all four angles equal to $90^\circ$, but its sides do not have to be equal, so it can be long and thin. A rhombus has all four sides equal, so any two sides that meet at a corner are equal in length too, but its angles do not have to be $90^\circ$, so it can lean over.

A square is the shape that answers yes to both questions. A shape with four right angles but sides of two different lengths answers no to the second, so it is a rectangle, not a square and not a rhombus. A shape with four equal sides but no right angles answers no to the first, so it is a rhombus, not a square and not a rectangle.

Ask both questions every time and write down the two answers before you name the shape. All angles $90^\circ$ and sides not all equal gives rectangle. Angles not $90^\circ$ and all sides equal gives rhombus. Yes to both gives square.

misconceptions.label: Names a trapezium or a kite without checking its property
misconceptions.description: The student picks trapezium or kite for a shape that does not pass that name's test, because the shape as a whole seems to suit the name, without checking for a pair of parallel opposite sides or for two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
misconceptions.signal: Trapezium for a shape with no parallel sides, or kite for a shape that does not have two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

refutation.text_md: You picked a special name because the shape as a whole seemed to fit it, and that is a sensible place to start. But a special name has to be earned by a property: each one comes with something you can check, and the shape has to pass that check.

A trapezium needs a pair of opposite sides that are parallel. To test it, make a quick sketch and extend each pair of opposite sides: lines that meet at a point are not parallel. If both pairs meet, the shape has no parallel sides, so it cannot be a trapezium.

A kite needs two pairs of adjacent sides, meaning sides that meet at a corner, with the two sides in each pair equal in length. Compare the lengths of the sides that meet at each corner: if they are not equal in two pairs, it is not a kite.

So a four-sided shape with no parallel sides and no equal sides passes neither test, and the only name that fits is quadrilateral. And a shape whose two pairs of adjacent sides are equal, but whose opposite sides are not parallel, is a kite, not a trapezium.
Before you name a shape, run the tests in order. Is any pair of opposite sides parallel? If not, are both pairs of adjacent sides equal? A shape that passes neither is only a quadrilateral.

misconceptions.label: Thinks a shape can have only one name
misconceptions.description: The student treats rectangle, square, rhombus, parallelogram and kite as separate boxes, so says a rectangle or a square is not a parallelogram, or a rhombus is not a kite, instead of seeing that a shape with extra properties still belongs to the broader group.
misconceptions.signal: Calls a statement such as 'a rectangle is a parallelogram', 'a square is a parallelogram' or 'a rhombus is a kite' false, or lists only the single most specific name when asked for all the names of a shape.

refutation.text_md: You're treating each name as its own box, so that a shape can only be one thing. That's a fair first instinct, because the usual pictures of these shapes look so different from one another. But a name is really a list of properties, and a shape belongs to every group whose list it satisfies.

A parallelogram is a four-sided shape with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. A rectangle has both pairs of opposite sides parallel too, so it passes the parallelogram test, and then it adds one extra property: all its interior angles are $90^\circ$. A square passes the same test in the same way. Each is a parallelogram with something extra.

The same goes for kite and rhombus. A kite needs two pairs of adjacent sides that are equal in length. A rhombus has all four sides equal, so both of its pairs of adjacent sides are equal and it passes the kite test. It is a kite that also has a pair of equal opposite sides.
A square shows how far this goes: it passes the tests for rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, kite and quadrilateral, so every one of those names applies to it as well as 'square'.

When a statement says one shape 'is' another, don't ask whether it looks like the usual picture of that shape. Ask whether it passes that shape's test. If it does, the statement is true. When you are asked to list all the names, test each name in turn and keep every one the shape passes.

misconceptions.label: Puts the factor of 2 on the wrong segment
misconceptions.description: The student compares the right two segments but uses the 2:1 ratio the wrong way round: doubling the line joining the mid-points when it should be halved from the third side, or halving the third side when it should be doubled.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is four times too big or four times too small, as if the long and short segments had swapped places.

refutation.text_md: You picked the right two segments to compare: the line joining the mid-points of two sides, and the third side of the triangle. The slip is in which of the two is the long one, so the factor of 2 ended up on the wrong segment.

The mid-point theorem says the line joining the mid-points is half the length of the third side. Said the other way round, the third side is twice as long as that line, a ratio of $2:1$. The third side is the long one and the line inside the triangle is the short one.

Check it with a case. If the third side is $6$ and the line joining the mid-points is $x$, then $6=2x$, so $x=\tfrac12\times 6=3$. Doubling instead would give $12$, a line inside the triangle that is longer than the side it is half of, which cannot be right.

It works the same the other way. If the line joining the mid-points is $3$ and you need the third side, then third side $=2\times 3=6$. Halving would give $1.5$, a third side shorter than the line inside it.

Before you calculate, write it as $\text{third side}=2\times(\text{line joining the mid-points})$ and put the given length in the right place. Then solve, and check that the third side comes out bigger than the line inside.

If the mid-line is 3, the third side is 2 x 3 = 6, and halving gives 1.5, which is four times too small. This matches the canonical method (third side = 2 x mid-line, then solve) and the final answers.
